summary: Zack Proser, an engineer on WorkOS's Applied AI team, frames AI developer burnout: agents are so powerful that developers exhaust themselves by 11am despite unprecedented productivity. The bottleneck is not agent capability but human attention, which degrades under load—Simon Willison's four parallel agents exemplify this. Proser illustrates with a bug-fix story where Claude Code, given MCP access to Slack and Linear, completed and verified its own work in a closed loop. His four-layer stack: signal layers (agents reading Slack/Linear so you don't), voice-first flows (184 wpm enabling parallel workflows), remote control (monitoring sessions from a phone on LTE), and system self-improvement (agents analyzing JSONL conversation history for patterns and missing skills). For JSONL management, hooks triggered at session end or PR merge can save key struggles into separate stores like Obsidian or markdown files for weekly AI analysis prompted to hunt for inefficiencies and churn. Three verification gates—lint/build, browser click-through, and constitutional AI critic—ensure safety. The balanced day starts with deep focus to queue work, then transitions to phone-based monitoring. An Oura ring via MCP lets Claude factor in sleep data. For night-shift work, Proser experiments with cron jobs and OpenClaw, reviewing outputs in the morning and merging only a small percentage; he envisions Linear tickets tagged "agent ready" with 15-minute loops running day and night. Voice workflows span Claude Code speech input with text output, OpenAI advanced voice mode for 2-hour brainstorming walks, and OpenClaw on Twilio for nighttime voice calls to set next-day tasks. For complex multi-stack features, he recommends git worktrees for parallelism, agent teams with clearly defined prompts, and heavier reliance on verification gates and CI, acknowledging harnesses are still evolving. Early-career developers should master fundamentals before delegating to AI.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the problem of AI developer burnout
sections.summary: Proser introduces himself as a WorkOS engineer and frames the core problem: despite unprecedented productivity with AI coding agents, developers are exhausted and adrenaline-dumping, with context switching now worse than ever. He asks the audience to raise hands if they feel fried by 11am despite getting more done.

sections.title: A concrete example of using AI agents for bug fixing
sections.summary: Proser describes a bug in a Slack blog bot's sentence case enforcer mangling acronyms like SKIM and SSO. He gave Claude Code MCP access to Slack and Linear, instructed it to fix and verify its own work, and returned to a completed loop. He notes this felt incredible but also scared him because there is no ceiling to agent scaling while the human nervous system remains ancient.

sections.title: The bottleneck: human attention vs. infinite agent scalability
sections.summary: Proser articulates that agents are not the bottleneck—they can scale infinitely, especially with cloud API access—and can match verification criteria. The hard constraint is human attention, which degrades under load. He cites Simon Willison being wiped out by 11am with four parallel agents and stresses that finding personal balance is now an individual responsibility. Humans still hold judgment and taste.

sections.title: The proposed stack for sustainable AI development
sections.summary: Proser outlines a four-layer stack: signal layers for managing notifications and context, voice-first flows for coding efficiency, remote control for monitoring agents away from the desk, and system self-improvement using stored conversation history.

sections.title: The Signal Layer: Managing notifications and context switching
sections.summary: Proser explains signal layers: agents read Slack and Linear on a loop via MCP, deduplicating asks and surfacing only high-priority items. This prevents the 80% likelihood of distraction when manually opening Slack, allowing the developer to maintain focus on key work.

sections.title: Voice-first flows for coding efficiency
sections.summary: Proser advocates voice-first coding, noting he reaches 184 wpm versus his previous 90 wpm typing. This enables parallel workflows across multiple cursor windows and Claude tabs, with agents often running while a traditional developer is still typing their first prompt.

sections.title: The Shower Principle and Remote Control for agents
sections.summary: Proser explains the shower principle: focus mode (at IDE, typing) versus diffuse mode (walking away, subconscious churning). Remote control in Claude Code bridges these—a session started at a desk can be monitored and directed from a phone on LTE miles away, so walking away no longer means stopping work.

sections.title: Remote control benefits and verification gates
sections.summary: Proser elaborates on physical benefits of walking away from the desk and recounts filming a 32-minute film proving you can review PRs from your phone in the woods. He then introduces three verification gates: gate one is minimal lint, build, and unit tests with hooks; gate two is browser click-through verification using Chrome use and computer use; gate three is a constitutional AI-style critic agent that verifies work against a constitution and gives actionable feedback. Speed requires safety.

sections.title: The new balanced developer workflow
sections.summary: Proser describes the balanced day: start with a deep focus session to queue backlog tasks and start feature work, then walk away and monitor from your phone on LTE. Agents handle natural language PR comments in GitHub mobile and often get it right. Without this structure, midweek random asks derail focus and by Friday you're wasted and disorganized.

sections.title: System self-improvement using conversation history
sections.summary: Proser explains that all Claude Code conversations are saved locally as JSONL files. A scheduled weekly or daily agent pass reviews these to find patterns where significant thinking tokens or back-and-forth were needed to eliminate ambiguity, then identifies missing skills and generates them. Claude Code has a built-in capability to build, evaluate, improve, and create bespoke skills from natural language prompts.

sections.title: Holistic well-being (Oura ring integration)
sections.summary: Proser connected his Oura Ring via MCP and gave Claude access to sleep data. Claude sometimes refuses to proceed on full tasks when the developer hasn't slept, suggesting deferring work to tomorrow. Proser sometimes overrides this but appreciates the prompt. He frames the default path as burnout turbocharged by LLMs and the intentional path as preserving yourself while directing agents to handle minutiae.

sections.title: Q&A: Addressing skill development early in a career
sections.summary: An early-career developer asks how to balance skill development with AI-assisted workflows. Proser advises: don't use AI to do something you don't already know how to do. Build foundational skills the hard way first, then use AI to accelerate once you have battle scars to catch hallucinations and bad ideas. LLMs can also help you go deeper by asking them to test you on gaps in your mental model.

sections.title: Q&A: Managing JSONL history and long-term conversation logs
sections.summary: An audience member notes JSONL files are not designed for AI consumption—they're long and messy. Proser says he has pointed Claude directly at them with success, but an alternative is using Claude Hooks triggered at session end or PR merge to save key bits—especially struggles and churn—into a separate data store like Obsidian or flat markdown files. An AI prompt then runs at week's end specifically hunting for inefficiencies and indications of struggle.

sections.title: Q&A: Night shift/background agent execution
sections.summary: Proser experiments with OpenClaw and cron jobs for overnight content generation, waking to review and merging only a small percentage. His envisioned system: Linear tickets for everything with subtasks for bugs and features, tickets tagged 'agent ready,' and a loop running every 15 minutes day and night churning through personal and company work.

sections.title: Q&A: Voice interaction and audio feedback
sections.summary: Proser describes using Claude Code with speech input and text output for most work, OpenAI's advanced voice mode for 2-hour brainstorming walks to sharpen ideas before generating a succinct transcript, and OpenClaw on Twilio for nighttime voice calls to set next-day tasks. He also discovered an open-source local voice tool called Ghost Pepper (similar to WhisperFlow) that doesn't use an API.

sections.title: Q&A: Handling complex, multi-stack features
sections.summary: A questioner notes parallel workflows work well for small bugs and UI fixes but grind to a halt for chunky features touching the entire stack. Proser recommends git worktrees so agents run truly in parallel without stepping on each other, agent teams with clearly defined prompts, and heavier reliance on verification gates, unit tests, and continuous integration. He acknowledges harnesses are still evolving and expects more complete solutions as models improve.
